entities.name: The Times
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Times, founded in 1785 in London, emerged as a pivotal institution in the landscape of Early Modern journalism and public discourse. As one of the earliest daily newspapers in the world, it played a crucial role in shaping public opinion and political discourse during a transformative period in Northern Europe, characterized by the Enlightenment and the rise of democratic ideals. Key figures associated with its establishment include John Walter, its first proprietor, whose vision for a newspaper that informed and engaged the public laid the groundwork for modern journalism.

Throughout its history, The Times has been instrumental in reporting on significant events such as the French Revolution (1789) and the Industrial Revolution, influencing both public sentiment and governmental policies. It was one of the first newspapers to adopt a more objective reporting style and utilize technological advancements such as the steam-powered printing press in the 19th century. The introduction of news reporting on a national scale and the establishment of foreign correspondents allowed The Times to provide comprehensive coverage of global events, thus setting a standard for journalism.

The legacy of The Times extends far beyond its initial publication, having influenced the development of the press as a vital institution in democratic societies. It has shaped the practices of journalism, including adherence to ethical standards and the pursuit of investigative reporting. The paper's extensive archive serves as a historical record of societal changes and has been a resource for scholars and journalists alike, underlining its enduring impact on media and public engagement up to the present day.
